title: MasterChef's Jyoti Vishnani on Building an Indian Kitchen Under ₹10,000
excerpt: The MasterChef India Season 4 contestant says a great Indian kitchen comes down to ingredients, technique and wisely chosen tools — not expensive gadgets.
body:
• Jyoti Vishnani, the MasterChef India Season 4 contestant turned Sindhi-cuisine champion, says a good Indian kitchen comes down to three things: understanding your ingredients, mastering your technique, and choosing your tools wisely.
  • Her path — from a corporate job in Ulhasnagar to professional kitchens, including a stint with Sanjeev Kapoor's Signature in Doha — taught her that technique outlasts equipment.
  • A practical ₹10,000 starter kit covers the real workhorses: pressure cooker, tawa, masala dabba, kadhai, belan-chakla, mixer grinder or chopper, and a solid knife set.
  • For diaspora cooks setting up from scratch, the same principle applies: spend on the few tools you use daily, skip the single-purpose gadgets.

MasterChef India Season 4 contestant Jyoti Vishnani has gone from a corporate career in Ulhasnagar to professional kitchens, a stint at Sanjeev Kapoor's Signature in Doha, and work assisting Michelin-starred chef Vikas Khanna. In a recent interview with Hindustan Times, she argued that after all of it — including watching AI move into commercial kitchens — the fundamentals of good food haven't changed: "understand your ingredients, master your technique and choose your kitchen tools wisely."

That philosophy, she said, evolved considerably after MasterChef. What began as a home cook's confidence became a deeper appreciation for regional ingredients, indigenous produce and the discipline behind professional cooking. And it is the lens she now applies to one of the most common questions new cooks ask: what do you actually need to start cooking Indian food?

From contestant to Sindhi cuisine's champion

Vishnani became one of the popular faces of MasterChef India Season 4, and she has since built her career on Sindhi cuisine — one of the subcontinent's most underexplored regional food traditions. She curated "Sindh Da Swad," a Sindhi food pop-up at Mumbai's Punjab Grill in 2019, has created content for the GotoChef app, and worked at POH by Chef Vikramjit Roy.

Her advocacy comes from genuine scholarship. She has spoken about researching Sindhi dishes through elders and chefs on both sides of the border, and about slow techniques like seyal — cooking in a dish's own moisture — that are disappearing because people lack the time. As she told India Food Network: "It evokes nostalgia... Most dishes are homey, but that doesn't mean they lack complexity. There are multiple textures and layers in each dish."

The ₹10,000 principle: tools, not gadgets

Vishnani's answer to the under-₹10,000 kitchen is not a shopping list of brands but a rule: choose tools you will use every single day, and skip everything that does one job. Applied to a starter Indian kitchen, the money concentrates on a short list of workhorses.

The non-negotiables are the pressure cooker (₹900–₹2,000), which handles dal, rajma, chana and rice in one vessel; a flat iron tawa for rotis and dosas; a masala dabba, the stainless steel spice box that keeps your everyday spices at arm's length while you cook; a deep kadhai for frying and slow curries; and a belan and chakla for rolling rotis. A mixer grinder or, for smaller budgets, a good veggie chopper (₹200–₹550) covers chutneys, masalas and prep. Add a chopping board and knife set (around ₹600), measuring cups and spoons (₹140), tongs, and a strainer, and the essentials are covered well inside the budget — with room left for a first round of staple spices and dals.

What to skip

The trap, in Vishnani's framing, is buying equipment before you have technique. Single-purpose gadgets — electric roti makers, specialised graters, yet another non-stick pan — eat the budget and the countertop. A well-chosen kadhai and tawa, by contrast, cover 90 per cent of daily Indian cooking. Spend the savings on ingredients: good masalas, fresh produce, and the grains and pulses that actually define the food.

Diaspora angle

For NRIs setting up a first kitchen abroad, the math translates directly. The same starter kit — pressure cooker, kadhai, tawa, masala dabba, belan-chakla — costs a fraction of a month's eating-out budget, and Indian grocery stores in most US cities stock them all. Vishnani's own journey from a modest Ulhasnagar home kitchen to professional stoves is the point: the cuisine rewards knowledge of ingredients and technique far more than expensive hardware.

What's next

Vishnani remains one of the few chefs bringing Sindhi food to fine dining — signature dishes like bhee ji tikki (lotus stem cutlets), palli dodo and thoom wara meya feature in her pop-ups — and her push for regional, indigenous ingredients shows no sign of slowing. For home cooks, her parting advice is simpler than any gadget: learn the ingredient, learn the technique, and let the tools follow.
